newsitem.title: UK: Drugs companies should warn of mixing, experts say.
newsitem.headline: Drugs companies should warn of mixing, experts say.

text.p: Doctors and drugs companies are debating whether people taking medicine should be warned against mixing it with illegal drugs, New Scientist magazine reported on Thursday.
It said the partner of a man who died after taking the illegal drug Ecstasy will press for an inquiry into whether the man's AIDS medication may have been partly to blame.
Philip Kay, who died after taking Ecstasy (MDMA) last year, was also taking Ritonavir, made by Abbott Laboratories Inc, to combat his AIDS, the magazine says.
His partner, Jim Lumb, says he was never warned that Ritonavir interferes with the liver's ability to metabolise drugs such as Ecstasy.
Kay died with abnormally high levels of Ecstasy in his blood -- Lumb claims because the Ritonavir prevented Kay's body from clearing it normally.
Pharmaceutical companies routinely warn about interactions with other legal drugs. But they do not warn users about illegal drugs such as Ecstasy.
Abbott said it had no plans to further investigate whether an interaction could have caused Kay's death.
Gordon Boyd, head of clinical development at the company, told New Scientist it would be difficult to issue warnings about mixing Ecstasy and Ritonavir.
"We would be seen to be condoning drug abuse," he was quoted as saying.
But Ray Brettle of City Hospital in Edinburgh said they could make warnings. "It's possible to come up with a form of words that makes it clear you're not condoning drug abuse."
Brettle and other doctors said research should be done into the risks of mixing drugs.
"Like it or not, a large percentage of the population uses recreational drugs," Katherine Bonson of the U.S. National Institutes of Health told the magazine.

Geoff Tucker, a pharmacologist at the University of Sheffield, said Ecstasy users were sometimes also taking Eli Lilly and Co.'s Prozac to counteract the depression that often follows use of Ecstasy, a form of amphetamine.
He said Prozac, or fluoxetine, inhibited the same liver enzyme as Ritonavir and the mixing could also be dangerous.
Lumb said he would ask a coroner's court to order an investigation into Kay's death next week and said Abbott should support it.
